questions.question: A support engineer needs every order to have exactly one customer while allowing a customer to keep years of order history. Which schema best enforces that relationship?
options: Add one mutable order_id column to customers
Add a non-null customer_id foreign key to orders
Store order IDs as a comma-separated customers field
Create an order_customer table without uniqueness constraints
questions.explanation: The foreign key belongs on the many side, so each order names one valid customer and the database can enforce ownership. A customer.order_id column is tempting but can represent only one order and would overwrite history.

questions.question: Users can join many projects, projects can have many users, and each membership has a role and joined_at timestamp. What should represent the relationship?
options: A projects.user_ids JSON array with roles stored separately
A users.project_id column that is overwritten when a user joins another project
Duplicate user and project rows for every membership
A project_memberships junction table with both foreign keys and a unique pair
questions.explanation: The junction row is the membership, so it can carry role and joined_at while a composite key or unique constraint prevents duplicates. A JSON ID array looks compact but weakens referential integrity and makes relationship attributes awkward to enforce.

questions.question: A product price changes from $25 to $30 after an order is paid. Finance must still reproduce the original receipt. Which fact should the order item retain?
options: The unit_price_cents actually charged when the order was placed
Only the product ID, followed by a lookup of the current catalog price
A copy of every current product attribute
No price because the payment provider can always reconstruct it
questions.explanation: The charged price is a historical transaction fact and belongs on the order item. Looking up the current catalog price is tempting because it avoids a copied field, but it rewrites the meaning of past orders whenever pricing changes.

questions.question: An orders table has 10 million rows. The main read filters by customer_id and returns that customer's newest 20 orders. Which index matches both the filter and ordering?
options: (status)
(created_at DESC, customer_id)
(customer_id, created_at DESC)
No index because only 20 rows are returned
questions.explanation: Leading with customer_id seeks directly to one customer's range, and created_at DESC supplies the requested order. Putting created_at first is tempting but does not efficiently isolate one customer before scanning recent entries.

questions.question: A dashboard needs daily revenue in under 100 ms, while normalized order rows remain the financial source of truth. What is the safest optimization?
options: Move payment writes into the dashboard cache and delete normalized orders
Build an owned daily-revenue projection with lag monitoring and a rebuild path
Remove database constraints so aggregation writes are faster
Recalculate every order on every dashboard request regardless of scale
questions.explanation: A projection is a derived, rebuildable copy optimized for the read while normalized facts remain authoritative. Making the cache the payment source looks simpler at read time but turns a freshness optimization into an unsafe correctness dependency.

questions.question: A large production table needs a new region column that will eventually be required, and old and new app versions overlap during deployment. Which rollout is safest?
options: Add NOT NULL immediately and let old writers fail until they are redeployed
Delete the old representation, then deploy code that reads the new column
Add the column and trust a local migration without validating production data
Add it nullable, deploy compatible readers and writers, backfill and validate, then enforce NOT NULL
questions.explanation: The staged sequence keeps both application versions compatible while data is filled and checked. Enforcing NOT NULL first is tempting because it establishes the final invariant quickly, but it breaks old writers before they know how to populate the column.
